title: Reading to study: skim, scan, question
keyIdea: Good readers match how they read to why they are reading. Skim (title, headings, first lines) to get the big picture and a map of the page. Scan (hunt for a number, name or key word) to find one fact without reading the rest. Turn each heading into a how, what or why question, then read that part closely to answer it. Finish by covering the page and recalling: rereading and highlighting feel productive but help memory much less.

kid: You do not have to read every page the same way. First ask what the job is. Do you need the big picture, one fact, or a full understanding? Each job has its own way of reading.
Skimming gives the big picture. Read the title, the headings and the first line of each part. In under a minute you know what the page covers and where each topic sits.
Scanning finds one fact. Hold the thing you need in mind, like a year or a name, and let your eyes jump. Digits and capital letters stand out, so you can skip every line without one.

To study a page, turn each heading into a question. 'Why bees are in danger' becomes 'Why are bees in danger?' Read that part to answer it. Then cover the page and try to answer from memory. That last step is what makes it stick.
adult: This is the survey and question stage of SQ3R: survey, question, read, recite, review. Francis Robinson set out the method in 1946. It links to two English curriculum goals: retrieving and recording information from non-fiction at Key Stage 2, and reading for a range of purposes at Key Stage 3. Secondary pupils meet far more text than they can read closely, so choosing a strategy matters.

Skimming and scanning are not the same. Skimming is for gist: you read the structure (title, headings, first sentences) and ignore detail. Scanning is a targeted search for one item, so a reader holds a cue such as a number or a capital letter and skips anything that lacks it. Close reading then comes with a question, which gives the reader a goal and a way to tell when they have found the answer.

Common mistakes: many students start every text by reading word by word from the top, or skim when they need detail, then cannot explain it. Another is asking yes or no questions from headings, which close down thinking. The biggest is trusting rereading and highlighting. Dunlosky and colleagues (2013) rated both low in usefulness, while practice testing, which means recalling from memory, was rated high.

In the lab your child skims a fact page and sees how few words give the map. Next they scan for a number while only the digits show. They turn three headings into questions and pick the one sentence that answers 'how far'. Last, they cover the page and answer three questions from memory.

familyTip: Next time your child has a chapter or article to learn, try a two-minute challenge. Give them one minute to skim it and tell you its main parts. Then ask for one fact they have to scan for. At the end, have them close the book and tell you three things before checking.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: skim a fact page, scan for a number, turn headings into questions, read to answer, then cover the page and recall.

practice.prompt: You need the date of a match from a long sports report. Which way of reading is best?
practice.hint: You need one fact, and it is a number. What stands out on a page?
practice.explain: Scanning is a search for one item. Dates are made of digits, which stand out, so you can skip every line without them.

practice.prompt: A page has {a} headings. You turn each heading into one question. How many questions do you have to answer as you read?
practice.hint: Each heading gives exactly one question.
practice.explain: {a} headings give {a} questions. Each one tells you what to look for in its section.

practice.prompt: The heading is 'How volcanoes erupt'. Which is the best question to read with?
practice.hint: Use the heading's own words and start with how, what or why.
practice.explain: 'How do volcanoes erupt?' matches the heading, and the section will answer it. A yes or no question, or a question that is too broad, gives you nothing to look for.

practice.prompt: A page has {a} words. Skimming its title, headings and first lines takes in {b} words. How many words did you not need to read to get the big picture?
practice.hint: Take the words you skimmed away from the whole page.
practice.explain: {a} − {b} = {=a-b}. Skimming skipped {=a-b} words but still gave you a map of the page.

choices: getting the big picture of a page quickly
pool.hint: Think about what you read when you skim: title, headings and first lines.
pool.explain: Skimming reads the structure so you know what the page is about and where things are. It is too fast to give detail.

choices: finding one fact, like a name or a number
pool.hint: Scanning is a search. What are you searching for?
pool.explain: Scanning is a hunt for one item. You keep a cue in mind and skip anything that does not have it.

pool.prompt: You need to explain how bees make honey in your own words. What should you do with that section?
pool.hint: Explaining needs every step, not just the gist.
pool.explain: Explaining needs full understanding, so read the section closely with a question in mind. Skimming and scanning skip the detail you need.

pool.prompt: Why turn headings into questions before reading?
choices: it gives you a goal and tells you when you have found the answer
it means you can skip reading
pool.hint: What do you do differently when you have a question to answer?
pool.explain: A question turns reading into a search for an answer. You know what to look for and when you have found it.

pool.prompt: Which is the weakest question for the heading 'Why bees are in danger'?
pool.hint: Which question can be answered with just one word?
pool.explain: 'Are bees in danger?' gets a yes or no answer and does not guide your reading. Why and what questions need real answers.

pool.prompt: After reading, which helps you remember most a week later?
choices: covering the page and answering from memory
pool.hint: Which one makes your brain work to bring the answer back?
pool.explain: Recalling from memory (practice testing) is rated high for helping learning. Rereading and highlighting feel easy but are rated low.

pool.prompt: You are looking for one person's name in a long list. What do your eyes hunt for?
choices: words in the middle of the page
pool.hint: Names start in a particular way.
pool.explain: Names begin with capital letters, so they stand out. Scanning uses a cue like this to skip everything else.

pool.prompt: Skimming one heading takes about {a} seconds. A page has 5 headings. About how many seconds does it take to skim all the headings?
pool.hint: Each heading takes the same time. Multiply by the number of headings.
pool.explain: {a} × 5 = {=a*5} seconds. Skimming the structure of a page is fast compared with reading every word.

pool.prompt: A section has {a} sentences. Only 1 of them answers your question. How many sentences only look close, or are about something else?
pool.hint: Take away the one sentence that answers it.
pool.explain: {a} − 1 = {=a-1}. Reading with a question helps you pick the 1 that matters and not be fooled by the others.
